data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nocturnal UHI gap is primarily controlled by differential longwave radiative cooling: urban materials have different emissivity and surface properties that slow net longwave loss after sunset, while rural surfaces radiate efficiently to the open sky. The single best cross-city modulator is the sky view factor (SVF), which directly determines how much outgoing longwave escapes to the cold sky sink versus being intercepted and re-emitted by building walls; cities with lower SVF have a larger nocturnal gap.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the nocturnal gap persists strongly even when urban and rural SVFs are comparable (e.g., in low-rise cities), the SVF-dominant claim is challenged.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If stored sensible heat release is found to dominate over radiative trapping in the nocturnal energy budget, the longwave-only mechanism is overturned.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If emissivity is similar between urban and rural surfaces, the emissivity component of this claim is unsupported.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"On a clear, calm night, radiative cooling is the dominant loss term. Urban surfaces with lower emissivity and lower SVF radiate less effectively to the sky: longwave emitted by the ground is partially absorbed by building walls and re-emitted back, reducing net radiative loss. Rural surfaces with high emissivity and unobstructed sky view cool faster. The nocturnal gap arises from this differential radiative cooling rate. Cross-city, SVF is the single best modulator because it directly scales the radiative exchange efficiency: lower SVF = stronger trapping = larger gap. Emissivity differences contribute but are secondary to the geometric trapping effect.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
